newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends mostly flat after erasing early losses.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends mostly flat after erasing early losses.

text.p: The dollar closed mixed against major currencies Tuesday amid growing belief that interest rates in Europe and Japan will soon rise, dealers said.
Investors had expected the dollar to rally after the German central bank, or Bundesbank, aggressively lowered a key short-term interest rate Thursday.

But the dollar has failed to rally and many market players have begun to price in eventual German monetary tightening. The dollar slumped against the German mark and the Swiss franc in overnight trading.
"People are still trying to decide whether the Bundesbank has made its final rate cut," said Seth Garrett, chief currency dealer at CS First Boston.
Higher foreign interest rates weaken the dollar by making assets priced in dollars relatively less attractive.
But the dollar later rebounded, erasing the early losses to finish nearly unchanged against European currencies.
The dollar closed at 1.4789 marks, up from 1.4788 late Monday. The dollar ended at 1.1931 Swiss francs, down from 1.1937.
Dealers cited profit-taking and technical support for the dollar's rebound against European currencies.
"We saw reasonable amounts of trading going through early, but there was little follow-through," added Garrett.

Interest rate concerns kept the dollar in a narrow trading range against the Japanese yen, with investors reluctant to trade ahead of a key quarterly business outlook survey called the Tankan due Wednesday.
Dealers expect the report to show a strengthening Japanese economy, which suggests Japanese interest rates will ultimately move higher.
"The Tankan is supposed to favour a recovery for Japan," said Greg Perman, chief dealer at Credit Commericale de France. "But I think people will sell the dollar tomorrow either way."
After failing to break through a key technical barrier at 108 yen, the dollar closed unchanged at 107.71 yen.

In late New York trading, the dollar got a minor boost from a Reuters Fiancial Television interview with U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who reiterated the administration's commitment to a strong dollar, dealers said.
"There was an extremely minute blip when he said that, but it's not really news. We know they don't want the dollar collapsing against the yen," Garrett said.
Shortly thereafter, the dollar fell by a similar amount when the U.S. Treasury announced the results of its latest auction of two-year notes, which some analysts deemed disappointing.
"The auction didn't go great and there's a fear that Japanese investors own a little too much of our Treasuries," Perman said.
While trading volume has dwindled in recent sessions, dealers expected a more active session Wednesday after the Tankan's release.
"People are waiting for that report to come out," Perman said. "It's been so dead in the last 48 hours it's not funny."
In other trading, the British pound fell to $1.5545 from $1.5576 late Monday. The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3682 from C$1.3707.
